turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doctor, I guess I'm here because my family and my friends, they just won't stop with this whole act they're putting on. They keep bringing out these bank papers, right? Stacks of them, printing them out from the computer, pointing at the numbers and saying, look, it proves nothing was taken, everything is right here. But they think I'm blind or stupid or something just because I didn't finish school. I know exactly what's going on. 

For over a year now, well over a year, I've known for an absolute fact that they are hiding my money from me. I see how they operate. They use all these little tricks to cover it up so the math looks right to everybody else. Like, suddenly there are all these extra bills lying around the house, or they start talking loudly about these fundraisers for people I don't even know, or they start making these big plans for trips. Who goes on trips when nobody has any extra money? It's my money. They're using all of that—the bills, the fake fundraisers, the trip plans—just to cover up the fact that they took it and they're hiding it from me. 

It's so obvious if you just pay attention to what they're doing. So I'm not going to just sit there and let them steal from me. I have to keep confronting them. Every single day, I ask them where it is, I call them out on their little trip plans, and I'm going to keep confronting them, over and over, until they finally look me in the eye and tell the truth. They only made me come see you so you'd tell me to stop, but I can't stop until they admit what they did.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, unyielding belief that their family and friends are stealing and hiding their money, maintaining this conviction for over a year despite being shown bank papers that contradict their claims.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Besides what you've told me about the money and what your family is doing, have you ever heard voices, seen things, or had other experiences that other people around you couldn't hear or see?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, I don't... I mean, I'm not crazy, doctor. I know what people think when they ask questions like that. You watch the movies, you see the news, and they always talk about people hearing voices or seeing ghosts or whatever, but that's not me. I don't have any of that going on. My ears work fine, my eyes work fine. I just see what's actually there. 

Like I was saying, it's the little things they do. I don't need to hear imaginary voices when my sister is standing right in the kitchen, talking loudly on the phone about some GoFundMe for a dog shelter in another state. Why would she care about a dog shelter in another state? She wouldn't. She's just saying it loud enough so I hear it, so I think, "Oh, that's where the money went." It's all a performance. But as far as, like, hearing things that aren't there? No. Never. 

I mean, sometimes I'll hear them whispering when they think I'm asleep, but that's real whispering. That's them coordinating their stories. I'll hear the floorboards creak, and I know it's my brother sneaking past my room, probably checking to see if I'm awake before he goes through the mail to hide the real bank statements. But that's real life. That's actually happening. I don't see things floating in the air or hear voices in my head. My head is perfectly clear, clearer than it's ever been, actually, because I finally figured out their whole scheme. So, no, none of that weird stuff. Just the truth of what they're doing to me, right in front of my face, thinking I'm too uneducated to catch on.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed belief that their family is scheming against them, coordinating stories, and hiding bank statements, which indicates persecutory delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices in their head or seeing things that aren't there.

turns.doctor_question: When you confront your family about hiding your money, do they agree with you that this is happening, or do they disagree and say it's not real?
turns.patient_response:
Agree? Are you kidding me? No, doctor, of course they don't agree! If they agreed, I wouldn't have to keep fighting them on this every single day. Like I was telling you just a minute ago, they completely deny it. They look at me like I'm the crazy one and they say it's not real. 

It's always the same exact routine with them. I'll walk into the kitchen, right, and I'll say, "Look, I know what you're doing, where is it?" And my mom will do this big, heavy sigh, like *I'm* such a burden, and she'll pull out those same bank papers. They literally keep a stack of them on the counter now just for this! And they point at the columns and say, "See? It proves nothing was taken. The math is right here." But they only do that because they think I'm too stupid to understand since I didn't finish school. 

They never just say, "Yes, we took it." They just keep lying. But I've known for over a year—a whole year of this torture—that they are hiding my money. And they have the nerve to stand there, telling me it's all in my head, while literally in the next breath they're talking about these fake fundraisers or planning some huge trip! I mean, how dumb do they think I am? You're telling me you don't have my money, but you're suddenly going on a trip? Or paying all these extra bills that just magically appeared around the house? It's sick, honestly. It's a sick game they're playing to cover it up. 

So, no, they don't agree with me. My friends do it too, they all just gang up on me and use those printed-out papers to try and shut me up. But it's not going to work. Like I said, I have to keep confronting them. I don't care how much they deny it or how many times they say I'm making it up. I'm going to stay in their faces about the trips and the money and the bills until they finally break down and tell the truth. I won't stop until they admit it.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient demonstrates a fixed, unyielding belief that their family and friends are hiding their money, maintaining this conviction even when presented with contradictory evidence such as bank statements.

turns.doctor_question: When you say your family is hiding your money and using these tricks to cover it up, do you think they have any special powers or abilities that normal people don't have, or are they just doing this through regular, ordinary means like anyone could do?
turns.patient_response:
Special powers? Like what, like magic or something? No, no, doctor, I'm not... I told you, I'm not crazy. I don't think they're aliens or witches or anything weird like that. They're just regular people doing regular, sneaky things. It's all just normal stuff anybody could do if they were greedy and deceitful enough. 

Like I said, they just use the computer. My mom sits there at the little desk we have in the living room, logs into whatever fake screen she set up, and hits print on that old HP printer we've had for like five years. It's not magic, it's just ink and paper. She probably buys the paper from Walmart, you know? Anyone can buy a ream of paper and type out a bunch of numbers to make it look like a bank statement. You don't need superpowers for that, you just need a keyboard. 

And my brother, when he's sneaking around checking the mail before I can get to it, he's not turning invisible or floating through the walls or anything. He's just walking in his socks so his shoes don't make noise, but I still hear him because it's an old house and the wood creaks. That's just regular life, doctor. It's gravity and wood and a guy in his socks trying to be quiet. There's no special abilities involved at all. 

They just use ordinary tricks because they think I'm ordinary... well, honestly, they think I'm less than ordinary. They think because I didn't finish school, because I didn't make it past the eighth grade, that I don't know how the real world works. But you don't need a high school diploma to know when someone is lying right to your face. You don't need special powers to set up a fake fundraiser, you just need a phone and an internet connection. My sister uses her regular old iPhone, standing right there by the fridge, pouring a regular glass of water, talking in her regular voice, just loud enough for me to hear about the dog shelter. 

It's all so basic. It's actually insulting how basic it is, when you really think about it. If they had special powers, maybe they'd do a better job of hiding the money, but they're just using regular, everyday lies. They leave extra bills on the kitchen table like anyone could. They talk about trips like anyone could. They're doing it right out in the open because they think I'm too dumb to put the pieces together. But I see every regular, ordinary little thing they do. I see exactly how they're operating, and I'm not going to let them get away with it just because they think they're smarter than me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses fixed, elaborate beliefs that their family is conspiring to hide money from them using fake bank statements and fake fundraisers, which are clear persecutory delusions.

turns.doctor_question: Over this past year or more that you've known about your family hiding your money, has anything ever happened that made you doubt this, or question whether it might not be true? Or have you remained completely certain about it the whole time?
turns.patient_response:
Doubt it? No. I mean... no, absolutely not. Why would I doubt it? They *want* me to doubt it, sure. That's actually the whole reason I came in, because my family and my friends just keep cornering me, day after day, saying the bank papers prove nothing was taken. They literally just gang up on me. They stand there, tapping their fingers on those printed-out sheets, looking at me with these fake, pitying eyes, trying to make me second-guess my own reality. They think if they repeat the lie enough times, I'll just break down and say, "Oh, okay, maybe I am just confused, maybe my brain isn't working right because I didn't finish school." 

But I'm not confused, doctor. Not even for a second. For over a year now—over a whole, exhausting year of dealing with this—I have known exactly what they are doing. I have known they’re hiding my money. How could I possibly question if it's true when the proof is right there in how they act? I watch them using all these sudden extra household bills, and those loud, fake conversations about fundraisers, and planning these big expensive trips, all just to cover it up! I mean, think about it. You don't just magically have all this extra money to go on a trip or donate to some random shelter out of state while at the same time claiming you didn't take a dime from me. It's insulting. They use all of these little tricks to explain away where the cash is going, and they expect me to just nod and smile and believe the fake math on their fake papers. 

If I doubted it, even for a minute, they would win. They would just take everything and leave me with nothing, treating me like some idiot who can't add two and two together. I see right through the trips. I see right through the bills. I see the whole picture perfectly clearly. 

So no, I haven't doubted it once. I know what I know, and I know I'm right. That's why I have to keep confronting them. I don't care how tired they get of it, or how much they try to convince you or anyone else that I'm the one making things up. Every single time they leave a fake bill on the counter, every time they mention a vacation, I am going to be right there in their faces about it. I am going to keep pushing and confronting them until they finally break down and tell the truth. Because they have it, and they know it, and I know it, and I'm not going to stop until they admit it.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses absolute certainty that their family is hiding their money and covering it up, explicitly stating they have never doubted this belief despite being shown contradictory bank papers.

turns.doctor_question: Over this past year or more, have you had any periods where your mood was very high or very low—like times when you felt unusually energetic and needed very little sleep, or times when you felt deeply depressed or hopeless?
turns.patient_response:
High or low? No, I don't... I mean, I'm not bouncing off the walls, and I'm not crying in bed all day, if that is what you mean. I feel normal. Well, normal for someone who is being robbed blind by their own family, anyway. 

Like, you asked about being unusually energetic or not needing sleep? No, I need my sleep just like anybody else. I try to get my eight hours. Sometimes it is hard to fall asleep right away because I am lying there in the dark, listening to the old wood creak, wondering if my brother is out there shuffling through the mail again in his socks, but that is just regular stress. That is just me being alert because I have to be. It is not some weird energy where I do not want to sleep. I would love to sleep peacefully! But I have to stay vigilant. I have to keep my guard up, because the second I let my guard down, that is when they will slip another fake bill onto the kitchen counter or plan another one of those trips. 

And as for feeling deeply depressed or hopeless... no, absolutely not. I mean, sure, it is exhausting. It is really, really exhausting having to fight your own mother and brother and sister every single day. It wears you down when people look at you with those fake pitying eyes and shove those printed-out papers in your face. But hopeless? Never. If I was hopeless, I would have just given up by now. I would have just let them take every last penny and let them win. But I am not giving up. I am angry, doctor, I am furious, but I am not depressed. 

They probably wish I was depressed. Oh, I bet they would love that! If I just stayed in my room crying all day and did not come out, they could sit at that little desk in the living room, print out all the fake bank statements they want on that old HP printer, and laugh about it while they pack their bags for whatever vacation they are paying for with my cash. But I do not give them that satisfaction. I get up every morning, I make my coffee, and I march right in there and confront them. So no, my mood is just... it is just what you would expect from someone dealing with this nightmare. I am just focused on getting the truth out of them, that is all.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses fixed, false beliefs that her family is robbing her and printing fake bank statements to steal her money.

turns.doctor_question: Besides believing your family is hiding your money, do you have any other strong beliefs about other people or situations that you feel certain about—like beliefs that people are trying to harm you in other ways, or that you have special abilities or importance, or that people are communicating hidden messages to you?
turns.patient_response:
Harm me? Like, physically hurt me? No. No, doctor, I mean... they're greedy, they aren't murderers. They wouldn't lay a hand on me. My brother wouldn't even know how to throw a punch if he tried, honestly, he just sneaks around the hallway in his socks. They don't want me dead or hurt, they just want my cash. That's it. 

And as for special abilities or being important... I mean, I just told you, I didn't even finish the eighth grade. I'm just me. I'm twenty-eight years old, I don't have a job right now because this whole situation is basically a full-time nightmare to keep track of, and I live in that creaky old house with them. I don't think I'm the Queen of England or, like, some superhero. Believe me, if I had special abilities, I would have used them to get my money back on day one, right? I wouldn't be sitting here in this office having to explain all this to you and defend myself. 

And hidden messages? From who? Like, secret codes on the TV or the radio or something? No, no, nothing like that. My family definitely isn't smart enough to invent secret codes, anyway. Like I said before, they just use regular, ordinary lies. When my sister is standing by the fridge talking about that out-of-state dog shelter, she's not speaking in some kind of spy code, she's just lying out loud to cover up where the cash went. It's not a riddle. It's just a lie.

I know you probably have to ask all these questions to see if I'm, you know, completely out of my mind. I get it, you're a doctor, you have a checklist of crazy things to ask about. But I don't have any of those weird thoughts. I don't think the FBI is tapping my phone, I don't think the news anchor is winking at me, none of that. It's just my family, and it's just my money. That is the only thing going on here. Just plain, old-fashioned, everyday greed. It honestly just frustrates me that we have to talk about superpowers and secret messages when the real issue—the actual, real-life stealing—is happening right in my own living room, and nobody will just make them stop.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient reiterates their fixed, delusional belief that their family is stealing their money, while explicitly denying grandiose, referential, or other persecutory delusions.
